title: Benchmarking OSS inference vendors on cost/latency
story_key: story|title:benchmarking oss inference vendors on cost latency
content_excerpt: This repo is in beta. We're still iterating on the methodology, so the approach and results may change. These results show speed (time to complete a research task) and cost for a single agent, not performance under heavy load, and providers differ in ways these tests won't capture. How fast and how cheap is each inference provider at serving an AI research agent using open-source LLMs? We record each model doing a set of research tasks once, using questions from Google's FRAMES benchmark, then replay those conversations on every provider. We measure how long the model calls take and what they cost at list price . Every model provider gets the same set of requests for a given model and task, so we're testing how each provider serves the model, not the model's ability to complete the task well. This is not a benchmark of model quality. Every model here completes every task, and we don't check whether its answers are right. The purpose of this benchmark is to compare timing and cost across providers, not model intelligence. Each model answers a set of multi-hop questions from FRAMES as a research agent, with tools to search and read Wikipedia. We only use tasks that every model is able to finish, and save each model's conversations along with the Wikipedia responses. The benchmark replays those conversations. For each turn, we send the conversation up to that point to the provider, time the response, and move on to the next recorded turn. The Wikipedia results come from the recording, so the timings only include model calls. Each model works through the tasks differently, so results are only comparable between providers serving the same model. Every provider gets the same settings for a given model (minimal reasoning, and temperature 0). After an untimed warm-up request, each provider handles one request at a time. Time spent waiting on rate limits isn't counted. Caching works normally within a task, and to see how much it helps, we also resend each task's last turn without the conversation cached. Each run goes through every task several times. A task that fails gets retried, and we only publish a run if every task finished. We run the benchmark monthly and on request, and the charts average every run from the last 30 days. Some runs only cover one provider, so providers may be measured on different days. Cost is the list price for the tokens each provider reports. Credits and discounts aren't included. Contributions are welcome. Feel free to open an issue o

Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot and any MCP client share one long-term memory of your decisions, preferences and project context, across sessions and across tools. ⭐ If Memro saves you from re-explaining your project, star the repo (top right): it helps other developers find it. Website · Docs · Discord · Voice demo · What broke wiring one memory into 4 AI tools Source-available: free for personal, research and other non-commercial use, including self-hosting; commercial use runs on Memro Cloud or a commercial license. github.com/memrohq/memro is the single public repository for Memro: the Go server, official SDKs (Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Go), the MCP server and the CLI. Adds Memro's MCP server and recalls the project's memory at the start of every session. See integrations/claude-code . In your assistant, say: "Remember that our primary database is PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector." Restart your session and ask: "What database and extensions do we use?" Run the full Memro API server and PostgreSQL with pgvector on your own infrastructure: (Note: The prebuilt image one-liner downloads docker-compose.release.yml with pinned ghcr.io/memrohq/memro:0.1.0 and ghcr.io/memrohq/memro-dashboard:0.1.0 images, available once v0.1.0 is published.) title: Show HN: Comemo – composite memory provider for Hermes Agent
summary: There are many memory providers that can be used externally with Hermes Agent. However, like many other AI agents, Hermes only provides one slot for an external memory provider. Comemo takes that slot and acts as a composite provider. How? It fans out memory writes to multiple backends such as Mem0, Honcho, and Supermemory. On retrieval, it queries the enabled providers, merges their results, and removes duplicates before returning them to Hermes. I intend to add support for more memory providers and eventually extend Comemo to other open-source AI agents with similar limitations.
story_key: story|title:comemo composite memory provider for hermes agent
content_excerpt: Composite memory meta-provider for Hermes Agent. Use Honcho, Mem0, and Supermemory simultaneously. Comemo is a composite memory provider for Hermes Agent. It runs multiple memory providers at the same time instead of one. Hermes lets you pick one memory provider. You can use Honcho, Mem0, Supermemory, or Hindsight, but only one at a time. Comemo sits in that single slot and writes to all of them at once. Reads come back merged and deduplicated. If one provider fails, the others keep running. Hermes only activates one at a time. This is a known constraint ( Issue #24770 , marked wontfix in core). The maintainers asked the community to build a composite provider as a catalog plugin instead. On every write, Comemo fans out to all active providers in parallel using a thread pool. If a provider fails, the write goes into a local SQLite retry queue and replays at the next session start. On every read, Comemo queries all active providers in parallel, merges the results, and deduplicates identical lines before returning to Hermes. Then run hermes memory setup — Hermes walks through enabling each provider and stores API keys securely in its secret scope. Restart Hermes after and Comemo is live. title: FEND: Far-End Detection in Outbound Voice AI Calls
summary: When a conversational Voice AI agent places an outbound call, the far end may be a live person, a voicemail greeting, an interactive voice response (IVR) system, or increasingly another AI system answering on the callee's behalf. Standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) reports only whether a human or a machine picked up, a design meant for human call centres, where one machine is as uninteresting as another. That single bit does not tell a Voice AI agent what to do, since leaving a voicemail message, navigating an IVR and holding a short exchange with another AI are three different actions and a two-valued label cannot distinguish them. In 1,000 randomly sampled calls from our own outbound deployment, a live person answered 48.1%, a voicemail system 44.6%, an AI 6.9% and an IVR 0.4%. Our proposed framework, FEND, reads the far end's audio and its streaming transcript and runs one detector for each automated class (voicemail, IVR, AI callee), with human the default when nothing fires, returning a single label within 20 seconds. On a public benchmark the voicemail components reach 100% accuracy without ever misclassifying a live human, where Asterisk's AMD misclassifies 30 to 66% of them. For the AI callee, acoustic features do not transfer across recording conditions, but speech timing does, separating AI from human at 0.952 ROC-AUC, because synthesised speech leaves far shorter gaps between words. On production traffic, separating a live person from any automated far end reaches F1 0.979, and only 2.9% of live people are given an automated label, the error that matters most for an agent acting on the result.

title: Agent-as-a-Judge
summary: Artificial intelligence has progressed from task-specific systems toward general models spanning perception, generation, reasoning, and autonomous interaction, making reliable evaluation essential for comparison, deployment, and post-training feedback. At scale, modern evaluation pipelines increasingly rely on LLM-as-a-Judge to produce scores, preferences, and critiques; in its fixed-context setting, the judge relies on the supplied evaluand and evaluation materials. Yet a reliable verdict may require evidence beyond the supplied evaluand and context---either because critical environmental states remain unrecorded in the static execution log, or because controversial factual claims require external verification. Passive judges cannot obtain that missing evidence before deciding, especially when evaluating agent trajectories, executable artifacts, or domain-specific reports. Recent work therefore develops active evaluators that seek missing evidence and update their grounds for judgment before deciding. We bring these advances together through Agent-as-a-Judge, focusing on how evaluators construct and control checking processes within the broader LLM-based judging landscape. We define the scope through evaluation-directed checks and the use of their results, covering both structured workflows and observation-driven control. We organize the design space by multi-agent collaboration, tool integration, memory, and planning, and show how these mechanisms supply the checks and evidence on which a verdict rests. We consolidate published scores and reproduce missing entries for key agentic judges; the comparison reveals uneven agentic gains and motivates dedicated agentic evaluation. We conclude by characterizing application demands and open challenges in cost, reliability, safety, and governance that condition trusted deployment of agentic judges at scale.

title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.

The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink. This is the third post in our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash series. The first post covered day-0 bring-up and kernel fusions. The second scaled the model to a GB300 NVL72 rack with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP. This post moves the same stack to Vera Rubin NVL72, which we introduced last month . Rubin opens up new avenues for optimization. We start with the hardware facts that shaped our work, then go through four groups of optimizations: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (vLLM, P/D disaggregation, Wide-EP) vs. GB300 NVL72. Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( GB300 source ). We measure performance with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs. We use the same methodology as in our previous GB300 post . For kernels and model forward profiling, vllm bench forward times exact prefill and decode batches through the real execute_model path, with real weights and real AgentX tokens. We A/B prefill kernels in loops that run for several seconds and report sustained numbers where they differ. Three properties of Vera Rubin NVL72 drove most of the decisions below. Where an optimization is specific to Rubin, we say which of them it relies on. title: How our GTM Agent builds consistent, high-quality sales artifacts
summary: Learn how LangChain built GTM Agent on Deep Agents to build high-quality, custom sales artifacts trained on business context.
story_key: story|title:how our gtm agent builds consistent high quality sales artifacts
content_excerpt: Over the last 12 weeks, our internal GTM Agent has saved LangChain's sales reps thousands of hours across its workflows. In that time, it generated 1,540 sales artifacts, which reps used to build by hand, one account at a time. These artifacts include customized account plans, proof-of-value documents, proposal decks, and onboarding plans. A powerful model can speed up artifact creation, one of the biggest time sinks in any deal, but can only take automation so far. What makes the biggest difference is everything built around the model: This post walks through how we used business context to build artifact generation with our GTM agent, and how we shaped it to fit the way LangChain sells. You can replicate this work on top of the Deep Agents harness. The primitives it depends on (a sandbox, skills, memory, and scheduled runs) are available in our managed version, Managed Deep Agents , so a team building something similar can get straight to capturing how its business runs. Earlier this year we wrote about how we built LangChain’s GTM Agent , which now runs a wide range of our sales and marketing workflows. It researches new leads and drafts personalized outreach for reps to approve in Slack, and every week it surfaces account signals like expansion opportunities and deal risks. Since reps were already using it every day, it was the natural place to take on one of the most time-consuming parts of their job: building sales collateral. That work was overdue for a fix. Inconsistent versions of the same document were showing up across the org. Account executives built proposal decks by pulling usage data into a chat assistant and assembling the deck themselves. The same work got repeated on every deal, and it looked different every time. We needed a way to standardize our hard-won lessons on what works without slowing anyone down. The third goal was the hardest to get right. Every stage of a deal has gates, or things that must happen before the deal can move forward, like naming an economic buyer or agreeing on success criteria. We track which stage every deal is in and which artifact helps clear each gate. But when this work was all manual, a skipped step usually came to light in a pipeline review, weeks after the rep could have asked the customer. Now that artifacts are filed through the GTM Agent, it can spot a missing one while the deal is still active. This workflow also gives our sales leaders a natural place to weigh in.
